draft.title: Choosing the passive voice
card: the doer comes first. "The storm destroyed the jetty." The subject does the action.

the receiver of the action comes first. "The jetty was destroyed by the storm." The verb uses a form of be plus a past participle, such as was destroyed. The doer can sit at the end or be left out: "The jetty was destroyed."
Writers choose the passive for effect. It puts the focus on what happened, as in "The window was smashed." It also sounds impersonal and formal, as in a science report: "The mixture was heated."
Leaving out the doer can also hide who was responsible. "Mistakes were made" says nothing about who made them.
draft.remember: The passive is a choice: it can shift focus to the event, sound impersonal, or leave the doer unnamed.

a.q: A student writes: "The pond water was tested for acidity." Why might the writer choose the passive here?
opts: It sounds impersonal, as a report should
It names the person who did the testing
It makes the action feel fast and tense
It puts the doer at the start of the sentence
a.why: The passive leaves out the tester and keeps the tone impersonal, which suits a science report. It does not name the doer, so the option claiming it does is wrong.
a.clue: Think about who is missing from the sentence, and what kind of text this is.

b.q: A council statement reads: "The footpath was left unrepaired for two years." What effect does the passive voice have here?
opts: It leaves out who was responsible for the neglect
It names the council as the one who failed
It makes the sentence active and direct
It puts the focus on the person who complained
b.why: The doer is left out, so the sentence does not say who failed to repair the path. The option about naming the council is tempting, but the passive here does not name anyone.
b.clue: Look for who is named as the doer in the sentence.

a.best: It sounds impersonal, as a report should

b.best: It leaves out who was responsible for the neglect
